course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Revolutions

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment

questions.prompt: Labor unions were formed mainly to
choices: bargain with governments for grants of land in the colonies
bargain with employers for better wages and conditions
help factory owners lower wages
replace workers with machines

questions.distinguisher: Unions bargained with employers about work, not with governments about colonies.

questions.prompt: Marx and Engels argued that history is driven mainly by

questions.prompt: The British Factory Act of 1833 is best understood as a response to

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims about reactions to industrialization is most defensible?
choices: Governments refused to pass any labor laws
Responses were limited to machine breaking

All workers supported Marx's call for revolution

questions.prompt: Marx and Engels claim that factory work has
choices: made workers the owners of the machines they operated

made work more creative and satisfying
ended the division of labor

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, German political philosophers, Manifesto of the Communist Party, 1848
stimulusBlocks.citation: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party, English edition of 1888, trans. Samuel Moore, sections I and IV. Project Gutenberg eBook #61.
stimulusBlocks.note: The bourgeoisie are the owners of factories and capital; the proletarians are industrial wage workers.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles. . . .

The need of a constantly expanding market for its products chases the bourgeoisie over the whole surface of the globe. It must nestle everywhere, settle everywhere, establish connexions everywhere. . . .

Owing to the extensive use of machinery and to division of labour, the work of the proletarians has lost all individual character, and consequently, all charm for the workman. He becomes an appendage of the machine . . . .

Let the ruling classes tremble at a Communistic revolution. The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.

questions.explanation: The closing urges workers to revolution.

It warns ruling classes to tremble.
questions.distinguisher: The call is addressed to workers, not owners.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, Chartists demanded
choices: voting rights for all men
the destruction of textile machines
an end to the Factory Act
voting rights for property owners only
questions.explanation: Chartists demanded that all men be allowed to vote.
choiceExplanations: Chartists demanded that all men be allowed to vote.
questions.distinguisher: Chartists wanted the vote for all men, not only property owners.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.8 key concept: workers established labor unions and movements promoting reforms, and some governments responded with reforms
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing workers' movements and reforms in Britain, 1810–1900
stimulusBlocks.text:
Early workers' protests in Britain included the Luddites, who smashed textile machines between 1811 and 1816. Over time, workers formed trade unions to bargain for higher wages and shorter hours. The Chartists of the 1830s and 1840s gathered millions of signatures demanding that all men be allowed to vote.

Parliament responded with gradual reforms. The Factory Act of 1833 limited child labor in textile mills, and voting rights expanded in 1867 and 1884 to include many working men. Socialists argued that such reforms were not enough.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the change in workers' protest described in the passage?
choices: From reform demands to complete inaction by workers
From political demands and organized unions back to machine breaking
From machine breaking to organized unions and political demands
From unions to machine breaking and riots
questions.explanation: Luddites came first, then unions and Chartists.
choiceExplanations: Luddites came first, then unions and Chartists.
questions.distinguisher: The order is reversed: machine breaking came first.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the Self-Strengthening Movement aimed to
choices: replace the emperor with an elected parliament
end all contact with Europe
adopt Western-style government and end the role of Confucian values in the state

questions.explanation: It built arsenals and a navy while keeping Confucian values.
choiceExplanations: It built arsenals and a navy while keeping Confucian values.
questions.distinguisher: The movement kept Confucian values and the imperial system.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.8 key concept: as the industrial states grew stronger, some states, such as China and the Ottoman Empire, attempted reforms, with mixed results
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing reform efforts in Qing China and the Ottoman Empire, 1839–1895
stimulusBlocks.text:
After defeats by Britain and France, Qing officials launched the Self-Strengthening Movement in the 1860s. They built arsenals, shipyards, and a modern navy while keeping Confucian values and the imperial system. Conservative officials resisted deeper change, and Japan destroyed much of the new Chinese navy in 1895.

The Ottoman Tanzimat reforms, from 1839 to 1876, reorganized the army, courts, and schools along European lines and declared all subjects equal under the law. Critics complained that the reforms increased European influence without stopping the empire's loss of territory.

choices: abolished the army and relied on European troops
stopped all territorial losses in the Balkans and Africa
increased European influence without stopping territorial losses
ended legal equality for subjects
questions.explanation: Critics said reforms brought European influence but did not stop losses.
choiceExplanations: Critics said reforms brought European influence but did not stop losses.

questions.prompt: Which evidence in the passage best supports the claim that many British workers sought gradual reform?
choices: Factory legislation and the vote were won through acts of Parliament
Marx and Engels called for workers to overthrow capitalism
The Combination Acts were used to prosecute union organizers
Early factories employed women and children for long hours
questions.explanation: The 1833 Factory Act, the 1867 vote, and the 1871 union protections were gains made through Parliament.
choiceExplanations: The 1833 Factory Act, the 1867 vote, and the 1871 union protections were gains made through Parliament.
Marx and Engels called for revolution, the opposite of gradual reform.
The Combination Acts show repression, not workers' reform strategy.
Factory conditions explain why reform was sought but not how workers sought it.
questions.distinguisher: Marx and Engels addressed workers, but the passage says most British workers did not follow their call.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.8 key concept: workers' movements and government reforms responded to industrial conditions
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing worker organization and reform in industrial Britain, 1799–1871
stimulusBlocks.text:
The first factories of the late 1700s employed women and children for long hours at low pay. Workers who tried to form unions were prosecuted under the Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800, which Parliament repealed in 1824. Reformers pressed for change. The Factory Act of 1833 limited the working hours of children in textile mills and created inspectors to enforce the law. In 1867 Parliament extended the vote to many urban working men, and in 1871 trade unions received legal protection.

Marx and Engels, who wrote in this industrial world, argued in 1848 that workers should overthrow capitalism entirely. Most British workers, however, sought gradual reform through Parliament and their unions.

questions.prompt: The argument of Marx and Engels in 1848 is best understood as a response to
choices: Enlightenment demands for equality before the law for all citizens
mercantilist controls on colonial trade and manufacturing
the Napoleonic reorganization of the German states in 1806
class divisions and harsh conditions in industrial capitalism
questions.explanation: Marx and Engels wrote about factory workers, owners, and conflict between classes in an industrializing society.
choiceExplanations: Enlightenment ideals influenced them, but their 1848 argument targets industrial class conflict.
Mercantilism concerned state control of colonial trade and was in decline by 1848.
Napoleonic reorganization had ended decades before and was not the subject of the Manifesto.
Marx and Engels wrote about factory workers, owners, and conflict between classes in an industrializing society.
questions.distinguisher: Enlightenment equality shaped socialist thought, but the specific complaint in 1848 was about capitalists and wage workers.

questions.prompt: The repeal of the Combination Acts in 1824 is best seen as evidence of
choices: an end to child labor in the textile mills of Britain
the replacement of capitalism with state ownership of industry
a ban on all strikes and trade unions in Britain
growing acceptance that workers could organize to bargain
questions.explanation: Repeal removed the criminal penalties for forming unions, a first step toward legal labor organization.
choiceExplanations: Child labor was limited by the Factory Act of 1833 and was not ended in 1824.
Repeal did not change who owned industry.
Repeal ended the ban on unions and did not create one.
Repeal removed the criminal penalties for forming unions, a first step toward legal labor organization.
questions.distinguisher: The Factory Act of 1833 was a real labor reform, but it limited child labor and did not concern the right to organize.
